To compute a probability involving a normally distributed variable [MATH: X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),] it is convenient to transform [MATH: X] into a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}]

Content:
So, we have

[MATH: P(X < x) = P \left( Z < \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)]

Content:
where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1)] is a standard normal random variable.

sections.normalized_html:
Given a normal random variable [MATH: Y \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),] we have

[MATH: P(Y \geq y) = P \left( Z \geq \dfrac{y-\mu}{\sigma} \right)]

where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1)] is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have [MATH: \mu = 5] and [MATH: \sigma = 4.]

First, we transform [MATH: Y] into a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

[MATH: P(Y ≥ 2.92)|= P(Z ≥ (2.92 − 5)/(4)); = P(Z ≥ − 0.52)]

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

Now, we express the required probability in terms of [MATH: \Phi(z)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: P(Z ≥ − 0.52)|= 1 − P(Z < − 0.52); = 1 − P(Z ≤ − 0.52); = 1 − Φ(− 0.52)]

From the table, we know that

[MATH: \Phi(-0.52) =0.3015.]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: P(Z ≥ − 0.52)|= 1 − Φ(− 0.52); = 1 − 0.3015; = 0.6985.]

Finally, we conclude that

[MATH: P(Y \geq 2.92) = 0.6985.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The normal distribution has the probability density function

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)^2},]

Content:
where the [MATH: \mu] represents the mean and [MATH: \sigma] represents the standard deviation. To state that [MATH: X] follows a normal distribution, we write [MATH: X \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2).]

Content:
The graph of this probability density function forms a bell curve centered at [MATH: x=\mu.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ed91decbcec8ea6f361ae701047a47f0]

Content:
In general, the greater the standard deviation [MATH: \sigma,] the flatter the bell curve. Intuitively, this makes sense because the standard deviation represents how "spread out" the distribution is.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Transforming a Normal Random Variable into a Standard Normal Random Variable

Content:
To compute a probability involving a normally distributed variable [MATH: X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),] it is convenient to transform [MATH: X] into a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}]

Content:
So, we have

Content:
[MATH: P(X < x) = P \left( Z < \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)]

Content:
where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1)] is a standard normal random variable.

Content:
For example, suppose we have a random variable [MATH: X \sim N(1,2^2)] and we want to compute [MATH: P(X \leq 1.4)] using the following [MATH: z]-table:

Content:
| [MATH: z] | [MATH: \, 0 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.01 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.02 \,] |
| [MATH: \, 0 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.504 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.508 \,] |
| [MATH: \, 0.1 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5398 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5438 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5478 \,] |
| [MATH: \, 0.2 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5793 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5832 \,] | [MATH: \, 0.5871 \,] |

Content:
The [MATH: z]-table above shows the cumulative probabilities for a normal random variable [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).] In order to use the table to compute [MATH: P(X \leq 1.4),] we must first transform [MATH: X] into a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z] by [MATH: z]-scoring:

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≤ 1.4)|= P(Z ≤ (1.4 − 1)/(2)); = P(Z ≤ 0.2)]

Content:
According to the table, we have

Content:
[MATH: P(Z \leq 0.2) = 0.5793 .]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: P(X \leq 1.4) = 0.5793.]

---
